messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Roberto is a 65-year-old divorced Latino man who has spent the past eighteen years teaching special education at a public elementary school in San Antonio. He presents for an initial psychological evaluation describing a constellation of symptoms that have quietly eroded his quality of life since his military service decades ago, and which have recently intensified to a degree he can no longer manage alone.

Roberto served as an infantry soldier during a period of sustained combat operations, and the event he identifies as central to his current difficulties occurred during a patrol ambush in which his unit was caught in a narrow corridor under heavy fire. The chaos lasted less than four minutes by his estimate, but within it he experienced a moment of acute disorientation — a wave of dizziness so severe he believed he had been hit — followed by the acrid, metallic taste of blood and smoke that filled his mouth as he pressed himself into the earth. A comrade was shouting his name from somewhere he could not locate. He survived. Several men did not. What lodged itself most deeply was not the sound of the firefight, but the way the dizziness had made him feel utterly unmoored from his own body at the precise moment he needed it most, and the taste that accompanied it — a taste he associates, without entirely being able to explain why, with the moment he understood that death was immediate and indiscriminate.

In the years that followed, Roberto managed. He built a career, raised children, and told himself that what happened overseas was simply the cost of service. But the symptoms never fully receded. They changed shape. Certain experiences began to carry an almost physical charge: the lightheadedness that comes with standing too quickly, the occasional taste of something metallic in cafeteria food, and the specific social pressure of being asked to talk about his service — each of these became capable of pulling him, without warning, back toward the ambush. When these triggers arose, Roberto found that his body moved before his mind could intervene. He began avoiding situations that carried any emotional intensity, steering clear of heated staff meetings, parent conferences that might grow confrontational, or any gathering where he might be asked to speak about himself. He made a habit of positioning himself near doorways — in the faculty lounge, at school assemblies, at his daughter's wedding — so that he could leave without drawing attention. He also began talking about the event as little as possible, deflecting questions from colleagues and family with practiced brevity, because he had learned that even naming what happened was enough to set everything else in motion.

What Roberto could not fully articulate, but what became clear across the first sessions, is that these strategies have not quieted the threat he perceives — they have organised his life around it. He is in a state of near-constant environmental surveillance. In his classroom, he monitors the hallway through the small window in the door, catalogues the positions of the children relative to the exits, and flinches visibly when a locker slams in the corridor outside. Unexpected sounds — a fire drill, a dropped tray in the cafeteria, a car backfiring in the school parking lot — place him on a level of alert that takes the remainder of the day to subside. He has come to believe, with a certainty that feels self-evident to him, that he must always know where the exits are before he can allow himself to relax, because relaxation itself feels like exposure. This vigilance, in turn, makes the triggers more potent rather than less: the heightened state of arousal means that a slight dizziness from dehydration or a particular taste in his lunch can register immediately as danger, which sends him back to scanning, checking, positioning himself near the door.

The loop has tightened noticeably in the past year. A new principal introduced a practice of staff sharing personal stories at professional development days. Roberto has begun calling in sick on those mornings. Three colleagues have asked if he is all right. He is not, and he knows it. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last spring when a child in his class vomited and the smell briefly mingled with something that recalled the taste from the ambush — and Roberto found himself at the classroom door, hand on the frame, before he was conscious of having moved. What he most fears is that he is becoming unreliable to children who depend on him. What he most hopes is that he can learn to stay in the room.
